projects.name: Weeding Gantry Robot
projects.full: Weeding Gantry Robot — final-year research project (EEE4022S)
projects.label: JS
projects.blurb: Low-cost gantry that finds and sprays weeds on the device
desc: A low-cost, fixed three-axis gantry that photographs a crop bed, decides on the device which plants are weeds and sprays water at each one. It was built for the final-year research project at UCT with a Raspberry Pi Zero W, an ESP32-C3, a 5 MP camera, an 840 × 480 mm bed and a R2000 parts budget.

The Pi runs the terminal interface, the offline detection pipeline and the spray jobs. The ESP32-C3 runs closed-loop control of the three axes at 5 ms, homing, stall detection and a link watchdog. Controller gains were derived from step-test plant models and checked in simulation across their uncertainty range before they ran on the hardware.
highlights: 245 closed-loop moves ended within one sensor count (1.07 mm on X and Y); worst settling time 1.86 s against a 3 s limit.
Positioning within 14 mm of the command against a 20 mm requirement (a bound from six grid readings, not a precise measurement).
Detection scored on a spray-grid metric: F1 0.908 for segmentation against 0.654 for YOLOv8n. Per-image Otsu segmentation took 4.3 s on the Pi Zero W.
Limits stated in the report: the classifier was not trained on the planted crops, and the laser positioning test was not run.

projects.name: fpgasim
projects.label: V
projects.blurb: In-browser Verilog simulator with a Tang Nano 9K board model
desc: An in-browser simulator for the Tang Nano 9K FPGA. Write Verilog in a Monaco editor, run it through Icarus Verilog in an ephemeral container, and watch the board’s pins and waveforms without touching real hardware.

Every run is untrusted HDL, so it executes in a throwaway, network-less container with dropped capabilities and hard limits: 12 s of run time, 256 MB of memory, 64 processes, a 16 MiB waveform and 200 KiB of source. Requests are rate-limited per IP.
highlights: Board model with 62 pins and Gowin .cst/.sdc constraint handling, synced to the simulated waveform.
272–375 ms round trip from source to waveform over four live runs.
69 unit tests (about 0.4 s) and an embeddable view used by scope.io.

projects.name: mcusim
projects.full: mcusim — STM32 Blue Pill firmware simulator
projects.label: S
projects.blurb: Bare-metal STM32 firmware run in QEMU, shown on a board view
desc: A simulator for the STM32F103 “Blue Pill”. Bare-metal C is compiled with arm-none-eabi-gcc and run in QEMU inside a sandboxed container, then the GPIO activity is read back from a semihosting trace and drawn on a live board view.
It gives a fast edit-and-run loop for firmware exercises, and tests that need no hardware in the loop.
highlights: Board model with 44 pins, driven by a semihosting trace from the QEMU run.
357–469 ms round trip from source to trace over live runs.
68 unit tests; limits of 15 s, 256 MB, 128 processes and an 8 MiB trace per run.

projects.name: Scope.io
projects.full: Scope.io — interview prep for electronics engineers
projects.label: IO
projects.blurb: Interview prep with in-browser circuit, STM32 and FPGA simulators
desc: A LeetCode-style platform for electronics engineers. Pick a problem, solve it in an embedded simulator (CircuitJS for analog circuits, fpgasim for Verilog, mcusim for bare-metal C) and get graded automatically against a reference solution.

Grading runs on the server and takes the test configuration from the stored problem, so a user cannot choose an easier threshold. Analog problems use a blend of time-domain error (70%), frequency-domain error (20%) and key features (10%); digital problems need an exact cycle match.
highlights: Three simulators behind one problem page: circuits, FPGA and microcontroller.
26 problems written (9 CircuitJS, 9 FPGA, 8 MCU), 7 live on the early demo.
126 unit tests; Next.js, Firebase Auth and Firestore on free tiers.

projects.name: MCC Sizing Tool
projects.full: Three-Phase MCC Sizing Tool — Tharisa Minerals
projects.label: MCC
projects.blurb: Three-phase MCC sizing tool adopted at Tharisa Minerals
desc: In industrial electrical distribution, a miscalculated cable size or an under-rated busbar isn't just an inefficiency — it can mean a flashover, or an electrician who doesn't go home that evening. That stakes-level thinking shaped this tool.

I built a parameterised three-phase motor control centre (MCC) sizing tool in Excel that takes a transformer, a set of motor loads, their starting methods and feeder lengths, and returns full-load and feeder currents (including largest-motor inrush), voltage drop across feeder cables and busbars, the equivalent power factor of the combined load, and weekly energy consumption and operating cost per motor.

Every output is computed two ways — analytically from first principles, and from manufacturer tables (SANS 1507 cables, Austral Wright copper busbars, WEG W22 IE3 motor data) — with the percentage deviation between the two built in as an automatic sanity check.
highlights: Adopted by the Tharisa site engineering team as the baseline tool for all feeder studies.
Methodology report formally accepted by the engineering department.
Presented cost-comparison results directly to the project engineering team.
Built-in analytical-vs-manufacturer-data deviation check catches specification errors before procurement.

projects.name: SRAM Data Capture
projects.full: SRAM Data Capture (MAX10 FPGA) — Cybicom Atlas Defence
projects.label: FPGA
projects.blurb: FPGA capture of data from a legacy battery-backed SRAM
desc: A legacy embedded control system loads its boot and configuration data from a non-volatile SRAM (M48T35). The SRAM depends on a battery to keep its contents, so the data had to be read out without disturbing the system. I was tasked with extracting it without interfering with normal operation.

The constraint was timing: the SRAM presents valid data for about 10 ns, roughly 70 ns after Chip Enable and Output Enable go low, as observed on an oscilloscope. I designed a capture system on a MAX10 FPGA (DE10-Lite): a PLL making 200 MHz from the 50 MHz input, a 4-bit timer ticking every 5 ns, logic that fires the capture at the right count, and registers that latch the 8-bit data and 15-bit address. An 8-bit bus-buffer stage level-shifts between the 5 V SRAM bus and the 3.3 V FPGA without loading it.

On review for the public repo I found a timing bug in my own design: the timer ran freely, so the capture was only well timed for 2 of 16 possible arrival times. I re-armed the timer on every access, added a two-flop synchroniser on the enable lines and wrote a phase-sweep testbench. The fixed design latches correctly at all 16.
highlights: 200 MHz capture with 5 ns timer resolution against a 10 ns data window.
Phase-sweep testbench: 2 of 16 arrival times correct before the fix, 16 of 16 after (simulation).
5 V to 3.3 V buffer stage designed to avoid loading the SRAM bus.
Verified in simulation; not yet re-timed on the board after the fix.

projects.name: UDP Motion Sim Comms
projects.full: UDP Communication for a Motion Simulator — Cybicom Atlas Defence
projects.label: UDP
projects.blurb: Multi-threaded UDP client and server in C for a motion simulator
desc: Cybicom’s motion simulator needed a channel to exchange control and status messages with its instructor station. I built a bidirectional, multi-threaded UDP communication system in C using POSIX threads on Windows.

A client thread sends control frames with sendto() and a checksum; a server thread receives status frames with recvfrom() and checks the checksum; a main thread launches both. The frames are packed structs (24 bytes out, 42 bytes in), and the payload fields are anonymised in the public repo.
It was handed over with documentation. When I published it I added a socket-free test for the frame sizes and checksum, and fixed a bug where good frames with a payload sum above 255 were rejected.
highlights: Two-thread UDP client and server in C, with packed frame structs and an 8-bit checksum.
Host-side test for frame sizes and checksum truncation (6 checks pass).
Documented limits: Windows-only, no send pacing, and the checksum range needs checking against the interface spec.

projects.name: Simulator Mounting Rig
projects.full: Custom Mounting Solution for a Simulation Computer — Cybicom Atlas Defence
projects.label: CAD
projects.blurb: Parametric mount for a 4U simulation computer
desc: A 4U 19-inch COTS simulation computer needed to be securely mounted inside the instructor station of a motion simulator — but the rack-mounted unit was prone to sliding under the inertial forces the simulator itself produced, and still needed to come out easily for maintenance.

I 3D-printed custom measurement jigs (designed in Fusion 360, sliced in Cura) to accurately map the mounting dimensions, then developed a parametric hinge-and-hook system that secures the unit while keeping it serviceable. M6 bolts handle the shear and tensile loads, sized for the expected forces.
The mounting was verified through visual inspection and mechanical testing: zero visible stress on the unit, and full access via a single bolt release and hook rotation.
highlights: Designed and 3D-printed custom measurement tooling to capture accurate mounting dimensions.
Developed a parametric hinge-and-hook mount balancing security against inertial loads with easy serviceability.
Verified under mechanical testing with zero visible stress and single-action release.

projects.label: NET
projects.blurb: Restoring LAN connectivity across plant sites
desc: As a Network Engineer/Artisan vacation student, I worked on restoring and expanding Tharisa's network infrastructure across the plant — bringing critical systems back online, connecting new office spaces, and investigating Microsoft Cloud PC as a potential long-term remote-work solution.

The work was hands-on and infrastructure-first: fibre optic cable installation and configuration, switch-device connectivity, and troubleshooting LAN connections between devices and a central server across multiple sites.
highlights: Restored LAN connectivity between devices and a server across multiple plant sites.
Investigated Microsoft Cloud PC as a cost-reduction strategy for remote operations.
Expanded network access by connecting new office spaces into the existing infrastructure.

projects.label: E&I
desc: My first placement at Tharisa: shadowing and assisting Electrical Artisans and Instrumentation Technicians in their daily, routine work — inspecting and maintaining plant electrical equipment and control systems.

It was a ground-level introduction to industrial electrical maintenance, and the first time I saw, up close, why the fundamentals I was starting to learn at university actually mattered on a real plant floor.
highlights: Shadowed and assisted qualified Electrical Artisans and Instrumentation Technicians.
Gained first-hand exposure to routine inspection and maintenance of industrial electrical equipment.
First industry placement — the starting point for four consecutive years of vacation work in the field.

posts.title: Getting the 'why' right before the build
pars: It’s tempting to start building the moment a problem is handed to you. The tools are right there, the deadline is real, and typing feels like progress. I’ve learned to resist that pull.

Before I reach for a tool, I try to understand the fundamentals of what I’m actually solving. Getting the why right — why this approach, why this constraint matters, why the obvious solution fails — saves far more time than moving fast ever does.
It also means giving myself room to be wrong early, when being wrong is cheap. A wrong assumption caught on paper costs an afternoon. The same assumption caught in silicon costs a semester.

posts.title: What four vacation placements taught me before I could call myself an engineer
pars: My first placement at Tharisa had me shadowing electrical artisans, watching them inspect and maintain equipment I barely understood on paper. My most recent placement had me presenting a costing tool I'd built to the project engineering team. Four vacations apart, and the distance between those two versions of me is the whole point of doing this while still studying.

Each placement changed what I paid attention to. Network restoration taught me that infrastructure work is mostly about finding the one broken link in a system that looks fine from the top. The MCC sizing tool taught me that engineers don't trust a single number — they compute it twice, from different assumptions, and interrogate the gap between the two answers.

None of this replaces coursework. But it's the part of engineering that doesn't show up in a syllabus: what it feels like when a methodology report you wrote gets accepted by people who've been doing this for twenty years, and have every reason to say no.
